title: Wonhyo's skull
hookLine: Wonhyo drinks sweet water in the dark and in the morning sees it was in a skull: all is mind
carry: it was sweet in the dark

lines: A STORM ON THE ROAD TO CHINA.
cards: Two Korean monks, no longer young, are on the road to China to study. Night falls in a storm. They find shelter in what feels like a cave and lie down, soaked and tired.
In the dark, one of them, Wonhyo, wakes up desperately thirsty. He feels around, finds a vessel full of rainwater, and drinks. It's cool, and it tastes sweet.
He sleeps content. In the morning light he sees what he drank from: a human skull. The shelter is a tomb.
His stomach turns. And then something else happens.

teach.b: Wonhyo is sick at the sight, and right in the middle of the sickness he sees it. Nothing about the water changed overnight. Last night it was sweet; this morning it's revolting.

Only his mind changed. The story gives him words like these: when a thought arises, all kinds of things arise; when the thought stops, a cave and a tomb are not two. It isn't a new idea he cooked up in a tomb.
At Nalanda, some days back, this path sat with the first verse of the Dhammapada: all that we are comes from what we have thought.

teach.h: THE THREE REALMS ARE MIND ONLY.
teach.b: And the Mahayana sutras Wonhyo studied put it their own way: the three realms are mind only. Wonhyo had read those words. In the tomb he tasted them.
The story is told more than one way.

teach.h: A TOMB IN THE OLDER TELLING.
teach.b: One early Chinese telling, in a collection of the lives of monks, has the two friends sleep in what they thought was an earthen shelter and wake to find it was an old tomb, with no skull and no water.
The skull and the sweet drink come in later tellings, the version often told in Korea today. Either way, the point is the same: much of what makes a moment sweet or foul isn't in the thing.

teach.h: THE LABEL COMES A SECOND LATER.
teach.b: It's in the label stuck on it a second later.

teach.h: IT WAS SWEET IN THE DARK.
teach.b: A message from a name you dread. A stain that turns out to be paint. The water hadn't changed.

how: Korean Buddhists tell the story of Wonhyo's night in the tomb as a teaching on mind, and Wonhyo is honored in Korea as a great teacher and writer of commentaries.

o: a warning carved on a tomb to scare off thieves
a monk's relic kept in a Korean temple
the cup that was sweet at night and foul by day

p: the three realms are mind only

s: the water never changed. only what Wonhyo knew about it did.
one early telling has a tomb but no skull
a Chinese collection of monks' lives has the friends wake in an old tomb; the skull comes in later tellings.
Wonhyo invented the idea that the mind shapes things
the Dhammapada opens with it, and the Mahayana sutras he studied said it too.

games.q: you're Wonhyo. you drank sweet water in the night, and in the morning you see it was in a skull. what happens next?
o: you're sick, and that's the end of it.
you're sick, and in the sickness you see the mind made the difference.
you decide the water must have been poisoned.
games.why: in the story, the disgust becomes the teaching: the water didn't change. his mind did.

practice: Sit and watch what shows up: a sound, an itch, a memory, a plan. Each time, try to catch the tiny label that comes right after it, annoying, nice, boring, mine, and just notice that it came second, after the thing itself.

wordCard.voice: Wonhyo's skull. The vessel he drank from in the dark: sweet at night, foul in the morning, and the same water both times.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit citta: mind, the heart-mind that makes the sweet and the foul.

carryVoice: Your line: it was sweet in the dark. The sweet and the sick came from the same cup. Until tomorrow.
